messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Marsh is a 71-year-old single man who has worked as an insurance agent for nearly four decades, spending his days in a profession built almost entirely on conversation with strangers — a fact that has made his working life quietly, persistently unbearable in ways he has never fully named until now. He grew up in a small Ohio household in the 1950s and 1960s, the eldest son of a father who drank heavily and whose moods shifted without warning from indifference to violence. What Gerald remembers most clearly, even now, is not any single beating in isolation but the particular sequence of signals that preceded them: the creak of the back door, the sharp chemical sweetness of whiskey that entered the room before his father did, and then the waiting — a waiting so total it felt like the air itself had changed. His father was the person Gerald was supposed to trust most, and the abuse continued for years before Gerald left for college at eighteen, never to live at home again. No one in the family spoke of it. His father died in his seventies, unremarkable and unaccountable, and Gerald attended the funeral and said nothing.

For most of his adult life Gerald managed. He worked, he dated occasionally though never married, he kept himself busy in ways he understood as simply being industrious. It was only in his late sixties, after retiring briefly and finding the quiet of an unoccupied mind intolerable, that he returned to part-time insurance work and began to notice how much effort it cost him to sit across a desk from someone he did not know. He had come to believe, in a way he could not quite articulate, that strangers carried an unpredictability that was specifically dangerous — that anyone approaching him without established context was a potential source of harm. In his office, when a new client entered, he would feel his chest tighten and his attention narrow in a way that had nothing to do with the transaction at hand. He was certain, in those moments, that he needed to assess the person quickly, to read them for signs of what they might do.

Outside work, Gerald has developed a set of habits that have quietly restructured his life. He avoids television almost entirely, particularly news programmes or dramas involving domestic violence or family conflict, because images of that kind arrive in him somewhere below thought. He keeps his mind occupied at nearly all times — podcasts while cooking, the radio while driving, word puzzles before sleep — because the alternative, he has found, is that fragments of memory surface without invitation and then vanish just as abruptly, leaving him disoriented and unsettled. These fragments do not arrive as coherent recollections but as shards: a sound, a posture, a quality of light. And sometimes, with particular vividness, a smell — the same sweetish, stale alcohol odour that once meant his father was home, now capable of appearing in the middle of an ordinary memory as though it belongs there. He finds this deeply disturbing, that his own mind produces sensations unbidden.

He listens, especially at night, for sounds near his front door. He lives alone in a modest apartment and has for many years, and he does not entirely understand why the sound of footsteps in the hallway still tightens something in his chest. He performs small private rituals before sleep — checking the locks in a particular order, reciting a kind of internal inventory — that he knows, on one level, are not logical, but which he has come to feel are necessary. What frightens him most is not any external threat he can name but the sense that his own body has never been informed that the danger passed. He reacts, and then he watches himself react, and the gap between those two things has grown exhausting.

Gerald sought help after a client last spring arrived to a meeting smelling strongly of liquor. Gerald ended the appointment abruptly, citing an emergency, and sat in his car for forty minutes unable to account for his own response. He is not sure what he hopes for, exactly. He is 71 years old and has lived this way for a very long time. What he said, quietly, at the end of his first session, was that he would like to stop feeling as though the past has not yet finished happening.
